items.title: [Feature]: Map unsupported reasoning_effort values to the nearest level the chat template accepts
items.body:
## 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Some chat templates accept only a subset of the reasoning effort ladder and
raise a Jinja error on anything else. For example, the official
`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` template validates `reasoning_effort` directly against
`('xhigh', 'medium', 'low')`, so a request with `high` returns HTTP 400:
`Unexpected reasoning effort high. Supported types are xhigh (default),
medium, and low.` Meanwhile the `ChatCompletionRequest.reasoning_effort`
field accepts the full ladder
(`none`/`minimal`/`low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max`), and
OpenAI-compatible clients — agent harnesses especially — routinely send
`high` or `minimal`. The request validates at the API layer, then fails at
template render time. Today the only ways around this are patching vLLM,
forking the chat template, or rewriting requests in a fronting proxy.

Proposal: let the operator declare the levels the served model's template
accepts, and have vLLM remap any other requested value to the nearest
supported level:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B \
  --supported-reasoning-efforts low medium xhigh \
  --reasoning-effort-rounding down
```

Semantics (on the ladder `minimal < low < medium < high < xhigh < max`):

- `--reasoning-effort-rounding down` (default): highest supported level at or
  below the requested one; if nothing is at or below, the lowest supported
  level. With the set above: `high` → `medium`, `minimal` → `low`.
- `--reasoning-effort-rounding up`: lowest supported level at or above the
  requested one; if nothing is at or above, the highest supported level. With
  the set above: `high` → `xhigh`.
- `none` (reasoning disabled) always passes through and cannot be listed in
  the supported set — the mapping never toggles thinking on or off.
- Flags unset → passthrough, exactly today's behavior.
- Each distinct (requested → effective) remap is logged once as a warning.

The mapping applies at the serving layer (Chat Completions, Responses, and
Anthropic Messages APIs), so every derivation path a client uses converges on
the same normalization before the template renders.

There is in-tree precedent for the underlying concept: the Harmony path keeps
its own private `REASONING_EFFORT` mapping in
`vllm/entrypoints/openai/parser/harmony_utils.py` because GPT-OSS supports a
subset too. This proposal makes the capability declarative and general
instead of per-model-family.

I have a working implementation (small: one new helper module, two frontend
flags, wiring in the chat/responses serving layers, unit tests, docs) and
will open a PR if this is welcome.

## Alternatives

- **Explicit mapping strings** (`--reasoning-effort-map high=medium,...`):
  more flexible but more configuration surface and easy to misconfigure;
  the supported-set + rounding-direction form covers the real cases with
  two short flags. Could be added later if a concrete need appears.
- **Fix in each chat template**: templates come from model repos; operators
  can't always change them, and every template author would have to
  re-implement tolerant handling.
- **Client-side/proxy rewriting**: works but must be re-implemented per
  client/proxy and per derivation path (effort can be derived from thinking
  budgets, explicit fields, etc.).
- **Do nothing**: requests keep failing at render time with a template
  error that's hard to trace back to the offending request field.

## Additional context

Observed with an OpenAI-compatible agent harness driving a Qwen3.8 model:
the harness derives `reasoning_effort` values (`high`, `minimal`) that the
template rejects, and affected turns fail with the HTTP 400 above until the
operator patches the server or the requests.

Verified end-to-end on `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` (BF16): stock serve 400s on
`high` as quoted; with `--supported-reasoning-efforts low medium xhigh` the
same request returns 200 with `high` remapped to `medium`
(rounding=`down`) or `xhigh` (rounding=`up`, confirmed via the injected
reasoning-instructions block in the prompt token count), one warning
logged per distinct remap. Also verified `minimal` → `low` (400 → 200) on
a community NVFP4 re-quantization of the same model. Note: some
third-party re-uploads ship modified templates that alias `high`→`xhigh`
themselves; the official template does not, and `minimal`/`max` fail on
both.

items.title: [Bug]: MTP spec decode still advances the grammar matcher after termination when a structural tag is built (residual after #44297)
items.body:
### Your current environment

vLLM **v0.27.1**, Qwen3.6-27B-FP8, TP=2 (2× RTX 3090), `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`,
served via `/v1/chat/completions`. Spec decode enabled with
`--speculative-config {"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}`.

### Describe the bug

When a structural tag is built for tool calling **and** MTP spec decode is enabled, the
grammar matcher is still handed a token after it has terminated:

```
/project/cpp/grammar_matcher.cc:612: Warning: The matcher has terminated after
accepting the stop token, but is trying to accept new token with id 198.
```

This looks like a **residual of #44006 / #44297** rather than a regression of it. That fix
("Constrain bitmask and trim grammar advance at the reasoning boundary", merged 2026-07-04)
is an ancestor of v0.27.1, and the fatal half is indeed gone — no `Failed to advance FSM`,
no `grammar rejected tokens`, no terminated requests, no 500s. But token **198** is the same
token that appears in that issue's `grammar rejected tokens [198, 248069]`, and it is still
reaching a matcher that has already accepted the stop token.

### Conditions

Two things must hold together. Either alone is silent.

1. A structural tag is actually built — i.e. `get_model_structural_tag()` does **not**
   return early. That needs `strict: true` on some tool, or a `tool_choice` other than
   `auto`/`none`.
2. Spec decode is enabled.

3 tools, 3 trials per arm, walking that gate. Only `--speculative-config` differs between
the two columns; nothing else changed:

| `strict` | `tool_choice` | structural tag | warnings, MTP on | MTP off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| absent | `auto` | skipped | 0 | 0 |
| `false` | `auto` | skipped | 0 | 0 |
| `true` | `auto` | **built** | 3 | 0 |
| absent | `required` | **built** | 6 | 0 |
| `true` | `required` | **built** | 6 | 0 |
| absent | named fn | **built** | 6 | 0 |
| | | **total** | **21** | **0** |

### Impact

Modest, and I want to be accurate about it: **the tool calls themselves were correct 3/3 in
all twelve arms in both configurations** (36 requests, worker healthy throughout). At this
payload size this is log noise plus wasted matcher work, not wrong output. I have not tried
to find a size or shape where it becomes user-visible, so I cannot say it stays harmless.

Filing it because it sits in the code path a recently-fixed fatal bug came from, and the
warning suggests the trim at the reasoning boundary is not covering every path that advances
the grammar under speculative decoding.

### Reproduce

Serve the model with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` and
`--speculative-config {"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}`, then send any
tool-calling request that builds a structural tag — simplest is one tool with
`"strict": true` and `tool_choice: "auto"` — and watch the server log. Remove
`--speculative-config`, change nothing else, and the warnings stop.

Reported separately from #52741, which is about `strict` being rendered into the prompt and
is unrelated to decoding; raised there by @gaby, who is seeing these warnings independently.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 hangs indefinitely at startup during CUDA-graph capture on Ampere (RTX A5000, TP=4) — fixed by --enforce-eager
items.body:
### Your current environment

- vLLM version: 0.27.1 (`vllm/vllm-openai:latest` container image)
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`
- GPU: 4x NVIDIA RTX A5000 (Ampere, compute capability 8.6), `--tensor-parallel-size 4`
- Platform: bare-metal Kubernetes (MicroK8s), NVIDIA driver 595.84

### Model Input Dumps

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Startup hangs indefinitely — no crash, no error, no further log output — shortly after model loading completes, with the above launch command on 4x RTX A5000 (Ampere). Confirmed via multiple independent attempts (30+ minutes each, manually terminated) that this is not simply slow, but a genuine stall:

- Last log lines before the hang:
  ```
  Selected MarlinFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel for Fp8LinearMethod
  Using Triton/FLA GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128).
  Using FLASHINFER attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER', 'TRITON_ATTN'].
  ```
  (Then nothing — no further output, ever, across 30+ minute waits.)

- **Ruled out slow Triton autotuning**: re-ran with `VLLM_TRITON_FORCE_FIRST_CONFIG=1` (skips exhaustive autotuning). The process stalled at the *exact same log line* with no measurable difference in behavior, which rules out an autotuning-search-space explanation.

- **Ruled out a genuine deadlock/network-handshake wait**: inspected `/proc/<pid>/wchan` for every worker process across two independent attempts:
  - One worker consistently shows sustained ~16% CPU usage, growing linearly over 25+ minutes, blocked on `futex_do_wait` (thread-pool coordination primitive) with 109 threads.
  - The other 3 workers show near-zero CPU, blocked on `hrtimer_nanosleep` (a timed poll-with-backoff loop, i.e. periodically checking a shared flag), not a blocking socket read.

  Neither of these is a network I/O wait — this looked initially like a plausible (if very slow) real compile/autotune in progress, but see below.

- **Fix**: adding `--enforce-eager` (disables CUDA-graph capture and `torch.compile`) allows the exact same model/config to complete `init engine (profile, create kv cache, warmup model)` in **10 seconds**, and reach a fully serving state in under 2 minutes total. Confirmed via the engine's own logged `compilation_config={'mode': <CompilationMode.NONE...}` when `--enforce-eager` is set, versus the full CUDA-graph/inductor compilation config (dozens of `cudagraph_capture_sizes`, multiple fusion passes) when it's not.

This strongly suggests the hang is in vLLM's CUDA-graph capture / `torch.compile` pipeline specifically for this model's hybrid Gated DeltaNet attention kernel (`qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py`), on Ampere (compute capability 8.6) specifically — not in the GDN kernel's own Triton JIT compile (which still runs fine under `--enforce-eager`), and not a plain autotuning slowness.

### Possibly related issues

None of these match exactly (different hardware and/or different trigger point — during inference/load rather than at startup before serving any request), but they point at the same general GDN/hybrid-attention hang/livelock problem class recurring across vLLM releases and backends:

- #52551 — Qwen3.6-27B (dense Gated-DeltaNet) permanently hard-wedges the V1 engine (NVIDIA, triggered by large images/long multi-turn — not startup)
- #45929 — Qwen3-Next/GDN hangs at Triton compile (ROCm RDNA4/gfx1201, closed)
- #49203 — Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (GDN hybrid) intermittently livelocks under load (NVIDIA GB10/Blackwell, not Ampere)
- #43885 — Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 spin-loop during prefill burst (NVIDIA GB10/Blackwell)

Given the pattern across several different Qwen GDN-hybrid models, hardware backends, and vLLM versions, it seems worth asking whether CUDA-graph capture for this kernel family has been validated on Ampere-class (compute capability < 9.0) hardware at all, or whether `--enforce-eager` should be documented as a required flag there for now.

### Before submitting a new issue

- [x] Searched existing issues for this problem — found several related-but-non-matching GDN/hybrid-attention hang reports (linked above), none on Ampere hardware or at this exact startup trigger point
- [x] The bug is on the latest supported vLLM version (0.27.1)
- [x] I have provided the environment/reproduction details above

INFO [model.py:842] Disabled mm_prefix attention mode because multimodal inputs are configuration-disabled. ... ``` **Expected behavior:** no warning — MTP draft classes never process raw multimodal inputs (they consume embeddings produced target-side), so a missing multimodal processor on the draft config is expected and should not be reported as a fallback. **Root cause** (v0.27.1 line numbers): 1. `SpeculativeConfig` builds a separate draft `ModelConfig` with `runner="draft"` reusing the target's model path (`vllm/config/speculative.py:842`); `hf_config_override` rewrites `architectures` to `["Qwen3_5MTP"]` for `model_type in ("qwen3_5", "qwen3_5_moe")` (`speculative.py:516-525`). 2. `Qwen3_5MTP` implements `SupportsMultiModal` (`vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_5_mtp.py:212`) — intentionally, because the draft merges multimodal embeddings from the target. Hence `_ModelInfo.supports_multimodal` is true and `ModelConfig.__post_init__` creates a `multimodal_config` for the draft (`vllm/config/model.py:725-768`), so `is_multimodal_model` is true. 3. Since #48796 every `ModelConfig` calls `MULTIMODAL_REGISTRY.supports_multimodal_inputs()` via `get_model_arch_config` (`model.py:839`). For the draft config, `_get_model_cls` raises `ValueError` because `Qwen3_5MTP` has no `@register_processor` (`vllm/multimodal/registry.py:176-186`) → the warning is logged and `False` is returned → follow-up INFO at `model.py:842`. The check conflates *consumes multimodal embeddings* (true for these draft classes) with *needs a multimodal input processor* (never true for drafts; `vllm/v1/spec_decode/llm_base_proposer.py:148` already consults the **target** config for `supports_mm_inputs`). Scope: any MTP draft class implementing `SupportsMultiModal` without a registered processor — `Qwen3_5MTP`/`Qwen3_5MoeMTP` and the Exaone4.5 / MiMo-V2 MTP classes (same pattern). v0.27.1 is the first release where the path is reachable (#34110 added the interface flag, #35520 the warning text, #48796 connected the draft config to the check; still present on `main`). **Impact / verification** (2x RTX 5090, both deployments serving the model above): image requests succeed in both modes with semantically identical answers (both correctly read text embedded in a test image); MTP acceptance 83.4% (mean acceptance length 3.50). The target's mm_prefix bidirectional attention is unaffected (the runner reads the target config, `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:524`); `vllm/v1/spec_decode/dflash.py:89-90` even clears `is_mm_prefix_lm` on purpose for its draft path, so a text-only draft config is an accepted state. **Suggested fix directions:** - Preferred: don't create `multimodal_config` for draft runner configs (gate `model.py:725` on `runner_type != "draft"`) or skip/downgrade the `supports_multimodal_inputs` check for `runner_type == "draft"`. A grep shows no consumer of the draft config's multimodal state, and `runner_type` is resolved before the multimodal init block (`model.py:609`). - Alternative (larger): distinguish "supports multimodal embeddings" from "is a multimodal-input model" at the interface/registry level. Happy to submit a PR for the preferred direction if maintainers agree on the semantics. Note: root-cause analysis and on-box verification for this report were AI-assisted and reviewed by the filer. - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the documentation page, which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: FP8 on RDNA3/gfx1100 exceeds the 600 s engine-ready timeout on first start — no AMD_Radeon_Graphics tuned configs shipped
items.body:
### TL;DR - The official FP8 checkpoint (Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8) **loads and serves fine on a consumer RDNA3 card** (gfx1100, Radeon W7900 48 GB, `vllm==0.27.1+rocm723` on ROCm). There is no architecture refusal — community trackers currently report FP8 as "does not run on RDNA3", but it does. - The out-of-the-box failure is a **startup timeout**: for `device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics` the wheel ships **zero** tuned W8A8 block-FP8 configs (of 218 device-keyed configs it ships 76 for AMD Instinct and 142 for NVIDIA devices), so the default config is used and warmup **JIT-compiles the Triton GEMM kernels shape by shape**. First engine init measured **1474.26 s** — 2.5x the 600 s default of `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` — and the APIServer aborts. - The abort message says the timeout is "**often caused by slow weight loading**". Our weights loaded in **16.33 s**; the 23+ minutes between kernel warnings were CPU-side Triton compilation with the GPU idle. - `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=1800` makes it start. Once the on-disk Triton cache is warm, engine init is **49 s** and every later start is ~2 min — the cost is one-time per host (until `~/.triton/cache` is cleared). - **Asks:** (1) ship tuned W8A8 configs for `AMD_Radeon_Graphics` (mirroring the MI300X/MI325 sets); (2) cheap: mention cold-start JIT/config warmup as a cause in the engine-ready timeout error or the env-var docs; (3) secondary observation: the **first inference** triggers a further ~43 min of JIT staging that `/health` does not reflect. - **I have the hardware** and am happy to run whatever tuning/profiling procedure you point at and PR the resulting `AMD_Radeon_Graphics` JSONs, and to test any RC on gfx1100. ### Your current environment
Output of python -m vllm.collect_env (venv used for all runs below) ```text Collecting environment information... uv is set ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 Clang version : Could not collect CMake version : version 3.28.3 Libc version : glibc-2.39 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : N/A ROCM used to build PyTorch : 7.2.53211 XPU used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.3 (main, Mar 3 2026, 12:15:18) [GCC 13.3.0] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-6.8.0-79-generic-x86_64-with-glibc-2.39 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : Could not collect CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to : GPU models and configuration : AMD Radeon Graphics (gfx1100) Nvidia driver version : Could not collect cuDNN version : Could not collect HIP runtime version : 7.2.53211 MIOpen runtime version : 3.5.1 Is XNNPACK available : True ============================== vLLM Info ============================== ROCM Version : 7.2.53211-e1a6bc5663 vLLM Version : 0.27.1 vLLM Build Flags: CUDA Archs: Not Set; ROCm: Disabled; XPU: Disabled GPU Topology: single GPU, NUMA node 0 ============================== Environment Variables ============================== PYTORCH_NVML_BASED_CUDA_CHECK=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/torchinductor_root ``` Install (per the ROCm install docs): `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/` → `vllm==0.27.1+rocm723`; `transformers==5.15.0`; host ROCm userspace 7.2.1. CPU: 2x AMD EPYC 9334 (full `lscpu` flags and the rocm-smi topology table omitted for brevity; available on request).
### 🐛 Describe the bug **Expected:** `vllm serve` (or `api_server`) with an official FP8 checkpoint on gfx1100 either starts within the default engine-ready budget, or fails with a message pointing at the real cost. **Actual (measured on Radeon W7900D, gfx1100, 48 GB):** | Run | `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` | Triton cache | Result | |---|---|---|---| | cold serve | 600 (default) | cold | `TimeoutError` at 600 s mid-warmup; weights had loaded in 16.33 s | | cold serve | 1800 | cold | engine init **1474.26 s**, then `/health` 200, serving OK | | warm re-run | 1800 | warm | engine init **49.01 s** | | later starts (x3) | 1800 | warm | 49.10 / 49.11 / 49.19 s, server up in ~2 min | After unlock, serving works end-to-end (105/105 benchmark requests OK) — at untuned-config performance; see measured results below. #### Reproduce without hardware (2 minutes) Anyone with the wheel installed can verify the config gap that drives the cold-start cost: ```bash CFG=$(python -c "import vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.utils.fp8_utils as m, os; print(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(m.__file__),'configs'))") ls "$CFG" | wc -l # 219 (218 device-keyed JSONs + README.md) ls "$CFG" | grep -c MI300X # 28 (+ 24 MI325X + 24 MI325_OAM = 76 Instinct) ls "$CFG" | grep -ci radeon # 0 ls "$CFG" | grep -c 'N=16384,K=5120' # 0 — not shipped for ANY device ``` The engine-side lookup is a plain file-exists check in `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py` (0.27.1, ~line 830): the filename is built from `get_device_name_as_file_name()` — which on RDNA3 consumer cards is literally the torch device name `AMD Radeon Graphics` → `device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics` — and when the JSON is missing the code logs the warning below and **returns `None` (default config)**. Nothing is ever written back to that directory, so the cost recurs for every fresh host/venv. #### Reproduce on gfx1100 (~35 min, needs a 24 GB+ RDNA3 card) ```bash # fresh venv — a warm ~/.triton/cache hides the bug (init drops to ~49 s) uv venv /root/venv-fp8 && VIRTUAL_ENV=/root/venv-fp8 uv pip install vllm \ --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/ # 0.27.1+rocm723 # model: official FP8 checkpoint, ~28.7 GiB # HF: huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 # (we used ModelScope: modelscope download Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8) SNAP=/path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 # 1) default timeout → aborts at 600 s: /root/venv-fp8/bin/python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model "$SNAP" --served-model-name Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 \ --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --port 8199 # 2) unlocked: VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=1800 /root/venv-fp8/bin/python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model "$SNAP" --served-model-name Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 \ --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --port 8199 ``` (All measurements above were taken with `--enforce-eager` added to skip torch.compile/CUDA-graph capture; the cold abort also reproduces without it, with `torch.compile took 67.53 s` interleaved.) #### Verbatim evidence
1) Cold run, default timeout — aborts while weights were long done ```text (EngineCore pid=280186) INFO 08-17 01:42:46 [default_loader.py:430] Loading weights took 16.33 seconds (EngineCore pid=280186) INFO 08-17 01:42:46 [gpu_model_runner.py:5405] Model loading took 29.38 GiB memory and 17.353099 seconds (EngineCore pid=280186) INFO 08-17 01:44:23 [monitor.py:53] torch.compile took 67.53 s in total (EngineCore pid=280186) WARNING 08-17 01:44:23 [fp8_utils.py:851] Using default W8A8 Block FP8 kernel config. Performance might be sub-optimal! Config file not found at /root/venv-fp8probe/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/configs/N=16384,K=5120,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,dtype=fp8_w8a8,block_shape=[128,128].json (EngineCore pid=280186) WARNING 08-17 02:07:49 [fp8_utils.py:851] Using default W8A8 Block FP8 kernel config. Performance might be sub-optimal! Config file not found at /root/venv-fp8probe/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/configs/N=5120,K=6144,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,dtype=fp8_w8a8,block_shape=[128,128].json (APIServer pid=279547) TimeoutError: Timed out waiting for engine core processes to start. This is often caused by slow weight loading for large models. Waited 600s (configured by VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S). To increase the timeout, set the environment variable: VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S= ``` Note the **23 m 26 s gap between the two fp8_utils warnings** — that is one Triton GEMM kernel compiling (single CPU core pinned, GPU idle), not weight loading.
2) Same wheel, timeout raised — starts, and the cost is visible ```text (EngineCore pid=371418) WARNING 08-17 08:07:37 [fp8_utils.py:851] Using default W8A8 Block FP8 kernel config. ... N=16384,K=5120,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,... (EngineCore pid=371418) WARNING 08-17 08:31:17 [fp8_utils.py:851] Using default W8A8 Block FP8 kernel config. ... N=34816,K=5120,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,... (EngineCore pid=371418) INFO 08-17 08:31:42 [core.py:355] init engine (profile, create kv cache, warmup model) took 1474.26 s (APIServer pid=371094) INFO: 127.0.0.1:33878 - "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 200 OK ``` The warmup pass walks five GEMM shapes for this model (N=16384/K=5120, N=5120/K=6144, N=34816/K=5120, N=5120/K=17408, N=14336/K=5120); none has a shipped config.
3) Warm Triton cache — the whole cliff disappears ```text (EngineCore pid=378832) INFO 08-17 08:38:28 [core.py:355] init engine (profile, create kv cache, warmup model) took 49.01 s (APIServer pid=378511) INFO 08-17 08:38:45 [api_server.py:682] Starting vLLM server on http://0.0.0.0:8199 (APIServer pid=378511) INFO: Application startup complete. (APIServer pid=378511) INFO: 127.0.0.1:46230 - "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 200 OK ```
4) Secondary: first-INFERENCE JIT staging (~43 min), invisible to /health Even after a healthy start, the first completion request triggers more JIT compiles; the server answers `/health` 200 the whole time and a default-timeout client (ours: 300 s) just times out. Verbatim from the first served request on a cache-warm-start server: ```text (EngineCore pid=434612) WARNING 08-17 13:34:18 [chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:419] Cannot use ROCm custom paged attention kernel, falling back to Triton implementation. (EngineCore pid=434612) WARNING 08-17 13:55:59 [jit_monitor.py:135] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: _causal_conv1d_update_kernel. This causes a latency spike; consider extending warmup to cover this shape/config. (EngineCore pid=434612) WARNING 08-17 13:55:59 [jit_monitor.py:135] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode_kernel. ... (EngineCore pid=434612) WARNING 08-17 13:55:59 [jit_monitor.py:135] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: layer_norm_fwd_kernel. ... ``` The very first request (13:34:18) outlived the client's 300 s ceiling; the first fully-served response landed at ~14:17:41 — **43 min after the first request was sent** (the request that completed was issued 14:07:52 and took `total_s=608.536757`). Subsequent traffic is normal: a 16-request warmup burst after this returned all 200 in ~26–28 s.
### Root cause (as far as the code shows) 1. `fp8_utils.py` builds the tuned-config filename from the torch device name — on RDNA3 consumer cards that is `AMD Radeon Graphics` → `device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics` — and the wheel ships **no** JSONs for that name (the entire AMD set is Instinct-only). Missing file → warning → `return None` → default W8A8 config. 2. With the default config, `w8a8_triton_block_scaled_mm` JIT-compiles its Triton kernel for each distinct (N, K) shape during engine warmup. On this host each big compile takes ~20+ min of single-threaded CPU (GPU idle); the shape-by-shape walk (first warning 08:07:37 → init done 08:31:42) accounts for essentially all of the 1474.26 s engine init. 3. The APIServer's engine-ready deadline (default 600 s, `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S`, consumed in the v1 engine core client) expires mid-warmup, and the error names "slow weight loading" as the likely cause. 4. The Triton disk cache (`~/.triton/cache`) makes every subsequent start fast, and nothing writes tuned JSONs back — so the cliff is a **per-host one-time cost that looks like a hard failure** the first time. ### Proposed fixes (ranked) 1. **Ship tuned W8A8 block-FP8 configs for `AMD_Radeon_Graphics`** (gfx1100 at minimum), mirroring the shipped MI300X/MI325 sets. This is what the runtime warning already asks for, it removes the "sub-optimal default" path entirely, and it is the lever for the performance gap below. I have a W7900 and am glad to run the config-generation/benchmark procedure on it and open a PR with the resulting JSONs if you can point me at the tooling. 2. **Cheap message/docs improvement:** `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` is documented, but the timeout error's cause list ("often caused by slow weight loading") sends users down the wrong path when the real cost is JIT/config warmup on an untuned device (weights: 16.33 s here). One extra sentence in the error string or in the env-var docs — "first-start JIT compilation of untuned kernels can take tens of minutes on newly-supported platforms; raise the timeout or pre-warm" — would have saved us hours. 3. **Secondary observation** (same platform gap, different surface): the first inference after a cold start triggers ~43 min more of Triton JIT that `/health` does not reflect (details block 4). If preferred I'll split this into its own issue — keeping it here because it shares the root cause (no RDNA3 tuning artifacts shipped). ### Measured results after unlock (context for prioritization, not a complaint) `--enforce-eager`, temp 0, fixed 100-token prompt, 128-token generations, 5 reps per cell, non-streaming: | concurrency | aggregate decode tok/s | requests OK | p50 request wall | |---|---:|---|---:| | 1 | 0.612 | 5/5 | 209.2 s | | 4 | 2.301 | 20/20 | 222.4 s | | 16 | 8.730 | 80/80 | 234.5 s | For scale on the same GPU, llama.cpp with a Q4_K_M GGUF of the same model does 28.6 tok/s single-stream and 164.4 tok/s aggregate at c=32 — so FP8-on-RDNA3 today is ~47x slower per stream, which the tuned-config gap plausibly explains a large part of. Capacity is not the issue: 29.38 GiB of FP8 weights on the 48 GB card with ~19 GiB headroom. ### Related issues (searched; not duplicates) - #51136 — AITER not enabled on RDNA3 (gfx1100): same GPU class, different mechanism (INT8/Quark + AITER gating vs FP8 W8A8 Triton path here); complementary data point. - #35547, #32116 — same engine-ready timeout symptom class on NVIDIA (slow weight loading / DeepGEMM warmup). This issue adds the RDNA3/FP8 instance where the dominant cost is per-shape Triton JIT under a missing tuned config, plus the configs gap itself. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] I searched existing issues (linked above) and found no report of FP8-on-RDNA3 failing startup via untuned-config JIT with this mechanism. - [x] `collect_env` output attached. - [x] Repro is self-contained; the configs-gap part needs no hardware. Happy to contribute: tuning runs on gfx1100 → `AMD_Radeon_Graphics` config PR, and RC testing on this card.

items.title: [Bug]: V1 MTP max_model_len skip emits zero token IDs as drafts and causes 0% acceptance
items.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
vLLM: 0.27.1
Container image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1-x86_64-ubuntu2404
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120)
CUDA: 13.0.2
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
FlashInfer: 0.6.16.post3
Model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8
Engine: V1, synchronous scheduling, text-only
```

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

In vLLM 0.27.1, `SpeculativeConfig.max_model_len` is now consumed by the V1 legacy GPU model runner. However, when a sequence exceeds the configured drafter limit, the skip path returns zero-valued token IDs with shape `[num_requests, num_speculative_tokens]` instead of returning zero draft tokens for those requests.

The scheduler then treats those zeros as real speculative token IDs. On the next step, the target model verifies them, they are rejected, and the metrics continuously report drafted tokens with 0% acceptance. This makes the intended "skip speculation" path perform unnecessary verification work.

The current eligibility check also uses the batch-wide `common_attn_metadata.max_seq_len`. Therefore, one over-limit sequence makes speculation stop for every request in the same GPU batch, including otherwise eligible short requests.

Related issue: #52258 reports that `max_model_len` was not consumed at runtime in an earlier V1 version. This report is about the behavior after the runtime check was added in v0.27.1.

#### Server command

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 \
  --language-model-only \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \

  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2,"max_model_len":80000}'
```

#### Reproduction

1. Start the server with the command above.
2. Send a normal short request. MTP works and has a healthy acceptance rate.
3. Send a request whose tokenized context is longer than 80,000 tokens (we used approximately 115,000 input tokens).
4. Observe the speculative-decoding metrics during generation.

Sampling parameters used by the workload included `temperature=0.1`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`, and `presence_penalty=1.5`.

#### Actual logs

A short request immediately before the long-context request shows normal MTP behavior:

```text
(APIServer pid=1) INFO 08-18 02:27:46 [loggers.py:310] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 608.2 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 18.3 tokens/s, Running: 0 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.0%, Prefix cache hit rate: 37.6%

```

After the over-limit request enters generation, the draft count continues to increase but every draft is rejected:

```text
(APIServer pid=1) INFO 08-18 02:28:16 [loggers.py:310] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 33.5 tokens/s, Running: 1 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 19.1%, Prefix cache hit rate: 29.2%
(APIServer pid=1) INFO 08-18 02:28:16 [metrics.py:120] SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00 tokens/s, Drafted throughput: 66.99 tokens/s, Accepted: 0 tokens, Drafted: 670 tokens, Per-position acceptance rate: 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.0%

(APIServer pid=1) INFO 08-18 02:29:26 [loggers.py:310] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 33.1 tokens/s, Running: 1 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 19.6%, Prefix cache hit rate: 29.2%
(APIServer pid=1) INFO 08-18 02:29:26 [metrics.py:120] SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00 tokens/s, Drafted throughput: 66.19 tokens/s, Accepted: 0 tokens, Drafted: 662 tokens, Per-position acceptance rate: 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.0%
```

The drafted throughput is approximately 2x generation throughput, matching `num_speculative_tokens=2`, even though speculation should have been skipped.

#### Relevant v0.27.1 code path

`GPUModelRunner._input_fits_in_drafter()` checks the batch-wide `common_attn_metadata.max_seq_len` against `effective_drafter_max_model_len`.

When the check fails, `GPUModelRunner.sample_tokens()` currently creates:

```python
self._draft_token_ids = torch.zeros(
    1, device=self.device, dtype=torch.int32
).expand(len(self.input_batch.req_ids), self.num_spec_tokens)
```

`_get_draft_token_ids_cpu()` then returns those rows as normal lists such as `[[0, 0]]`. `Scheduler.update_draft_token_ids()` assigns that list to `request.spec_token_ids`, so token ID 0 is scheduled and verified as a real draft.

#### Expected behavior

- An over-limit request should receive an empty draft list (`[]`), so no speculative tokens are scheduled or counted for it.
- Ideally, the limit should be checked per request: in a mixed batch, eligible short requests should still use MTP while only over-limit requests skip it.
- At minimum, when the entire batch is over the limit, `Drafted throughput` should be zero and there should be no target verification of placeholder token IDs.

items.title: [Feature]: Detect and break exact repeating loops inside reasoning sections (spec-decode-aware ThinkingLoopBreaker)
items.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Reasoning models (observed in production with Qwen3.8-27B at high reasoning effort, MTP spec-3) occasionally fall into an **exact repeating token cycle inside the `<think>` section** and burn tokens until `max_tokens`. `thinking_token_budget` (merged in #34668) bounds the damage, but it is a blunt backstop: a budget large enough not to harm legitimate deep reasoning (e.g. 32k) still lets a stuck request burn 32k tokens before the forced reasoning-end fires.

Proposal: a **ThinkingLoopBreaker** that detects exact periodic repetition in the reasoning section and forces the `reasoning_end` token sequence early — same UX as budget exhaustion (thinking is never disabled; the model exits the loop and answers from what it has), but triggered by detection instead of a fixed cap.

**Detection** (CPU-side, in `update_state`, amortized):
- Only for requests inside a reasoning section, past `min_think_tokens` (default 512), checked every `check_interval` (default 16) new think tokens.
- Over the last `window` (default 512) think tokens, find the smallest period `p ∈ [min_period=4, max_period=128]` such that the tail ends in `min_repeats=3` exact consecutive copies of the p-token cycle (`tail[-p:] == tail[-2p:-p] == tail[-3p:-2p]`). Python list-slice compares run at C speed; worst case ~16k element compares per checked request per 16 tokens.
- Exact-match only: a ≥4-token cycle repeated 3+ times verbatim is a strong runaway signature; enumerations/lists are not periodic. Fuzzy/near-cycle detection is explicitly out of scope (that remains the budget's job).

**Enforcement**: identical mechanism to `ThinkingBudgetStateHolder`, applied at both call sites (main sampler and the rejection sampler's explicit hook), so it **works under speculative decoding** — which a custom logits processor currently cannot: `RejectionSampler.apply_logits_processors` applies only penalties/bad-words, `MinTokensLogitsProcessor`, and the thinking-budget holder, and silently skips everything else (`vllm/v1/sample/rejection_sampler.py` ~L334-338 on current main). #43672 proposes an opt-in contract to lift that restriction for custom processors; this feature is complementary and does not depend on it — it follows the in-tree precedent #34668 established for thinking-aware sampling guards.

**Config**: a `loop_break` block on `ReasoningConfig` (which already owns the reasoning token IDs), rideable via `--reasoning-config`; per-request opt-out via sampling params, mirroring `thinking_token_budget` plumbing.

**Shared care**: the forced-end path must respect implicit reasoning-end sequences (e.g. `<tool_call>` on Qwen3.5+) — see #44676 for the equivalent hazard in the budget path; ideally both guards share one think-section tracker so a fix lands once.

**Observability**: a `vllm:thinking_loop_breaks_total` counter and a per-request annotation, so operators can tune `min_period`/`min_repeats` against real fires.

### Alternatives

- `repetition_penalty`: distribution-wide quality impact, discourages rather than breaks, applies outside reasoning too.
- `thinking_token_budget` alone: works (and stays valuable as defense-in-depth) but pays the full budget before breaking.
- Custom logits processor via #43672 once merged: viable out-of-tree home for the same logic, but it cannot share the reasoning-section tracking the budget holder already maintains, and every deployment must re-solve spec-decode row mapping.

### Additional context

Duplicate-work check before filing: searched issues/PRs for reasoning/thinking loop detection and repetition breaking (none found); nearest work is #43672 (spec-decode contract for custom processors, open/needs-rebase), #34668 (merged; thinking budget under spec decode), and the budget-behavior bugs #39573/#39697/#44676/#50473, none of which cover detection. I have a draft implementation and will link a PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the documentation page

items.title: [Bug] DeepseekV4 cannot start on sm_121 (GB10): unguarded DeepGEMM call, and CutlassScaledMM.is_supported() ignores compute capability
items.body:
### Your current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev608+g99a10304d` (container image, aarch64)
- 2× NVIDIA GB10 (**sm_121**, 121 GiB unified memory each), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.173.02
- Two-node TP=2 via the built-in multi-node `mp` executor (`--nnodes 2 --node-rank {0,1} --master-addr … --distributed-executor-backend mp`, rank 1 `--headless`)
- Model: `MJPansa/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-NVFP4` (mixed precision: routed experts NVFP4, attention / shared experts / head not quantized)
- `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` and `VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` are set

Other models start and serve fine on the same two-node setup with the same image (Qwen3-235B-A22B-NVFP4, Mistral-Small-4-119B, Qwen3.8-27B-FP8), so the cluster wiring itself is good.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

DeepseekV4 cannot start on sm_121. There are two separate architecture gates that report "supported" and then fail inside compiled kernels.

**1. `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` calls DeepGEMM unconditionally**

`vllm/model_executor/kernels/mhc/tilelang.py` has three call sites for `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm`. Two of them are guarded:

```python
use_deep_gemm = is_deep_gemm_supported()
...
if use_deep_gemm:
    tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(...)
else:
    _tilelang_hc_prenorm_gemm(...)
```

The third one, inside `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` (the first-layer 2-D input path taken from `models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py`), is not:

```python
from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm

tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(
    residual_flat, fn_broadcast, gemm_out_mul, gemm_out_sqrsum, n_splits,
)
```

On sm_121 this aborts during `determine_available_memory`:

```
RuntimeError: Worker failed with error 'Assertion error
(/workspace/.deps/deepgemm-src/csrc/apis/hyperconnection.hpp:56): Unsupported architecture'
```

The shipped DeepGEMM extension only contains kernels for two architectures:

```
$ strings vllm/third_party/deep_gemm/_C.cpython-312-aarch64-linux-gnu.so | grep -oE 'sm[0-9]{2,3}' | sort -u
sm100
sm90
```

Note this happens **even with `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0`**. That env var does work — `is_deep_gemm_supported()` returns `False` with it set and `True` without it — but this call site never consults it.

A fix that works: guard the call and fall back to `_torch_hc_prenorm_gemm`, which already exists in the same file and implements exactly this contract (`out[0] = x.float() @ fn.t()`, `sqrsum[0] = x.float().square().sum(-1)`); the broadcast shapes line up as-is. It requires a single split, so `n_splits` has to be forced to 1 on the fallback path before the output tensors are allocated. With that patch the model loads all 48 shards and gets past this point.

**2. `CutlassScaledMM.is_supported()` ignores compute capability**

Past the first issue, DeepseekV4's attention input projections fail:

```
File "vllm/models/deepseek_v4/attention.py", line 493, in _run_parallel_input_projections
File "vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py", line 461, in apply
File "vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/BlockScaledMMLinearKernel.py", line 132, in apply_weights
File "vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py", line 320, in apply_block_scaled_mm
RuntimeError: dispatch_scaled_mm,
/workspace/csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/cutlass/c3x/scaled_mm_helper.hpp:17
```

The selection gate in `kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py` is:

```python
@classmethod
def is_supported(cls, compute_capability: int | None = None) -> tuple[bool, str | None]:
    if not current_platform.is_cuda():
        return False, "requires CUDA."
    return True, None
```

`compute_capability` is accepted and never used, so the CUTLASS c3x kernel is selected on any CUDA device and then rejects sm_121 in the C++ dispatcher. A Triton implementation exists in the same directory, but `use_triton` on `BlockScaledMMLinearKernel` only affects the input-quantisation step, not the matmul, and there is no env var to override the backend choice.

### Suggested fix

Both gates should consult compute capability rather than assuming Hopper/datacenter-Blackwell:

- `CutlassScaledMM.is_supported()` should return `False` on architectures without the compiled c3x kernels so selection can fall through to the Triton kernel.
- `is_deep_gemm_supported()` should reflect the architectures actually compiled into the extension (currently sm90/sm100), not just the env var — otherwise every DeepGEMM call site needs to be individually correct.
- `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` should be guarded like its two siblings regardless.

Happy to open a PR for the `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` guard if that shape of fix is acceptable.

items.title: [Bug]: Sleep-mode Level 2 wake does not reload speculative-decoding draft weights — silent ~2x decode slowdown, acceptance drops to 0
items.body:
# [Bug]: Sleep-mode Level 2 wake does not reload speculative-decoding draft weights — silent ~2x decode slowdown, acceptance drops to 0

## Summary

After waking a vLLM server from Level 2 sleep using the documented staged
sequence (`wake_up(tags=["weights"])` → `collective_rpc("reload_weights")`
→ `wake_up(tags=["kv_cache"])` → `reset_prefix_cache`), MTP speculative
decoding stops working entirely: every drafted token is rejected, and decode
throughput drops to roughly the no-speculation rate. **Outputs remain
correct** (verification rejects the garbage drafts), which makes the bug
silent — nothing crashes and no quality signal fires; you only notice via
throughput or the SpecDecoding metrics line.

## Environment

- vLLM: `0.1.dev493+g4d9600003` (installed); bug also verified present on
  current `main` (fetched `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` and
  `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py` on 2026-08-15 — `reload_weights` still
  iterates the main model's `named_parameters()` only, and `wake_up` still
  restores draft *buffers* only)
- GPUs: 2x RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (dense, FP8), `--speculative-config
  '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2,
  "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size":[[1,2,2],[3,16,0]]}'`
- Server flags: `--enable-sleep-mode`, `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`,
  kv-cache fp8, prefix caching on, custom all-reduce on
- PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0

## Reproduction (serving API)

```
# 1. cold boot with MTP spec decoding enabled; confirm baseline:
#    SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 2.6-2.8, ~110 tok/s decode

# 2. sleep level 2
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8000/sleep?level=2'

# 3. documented staged wake
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8000/wake_up?tags=["weights"]'
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8000/collective_rpc' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"method":"reload_weights"}'
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8000/wake_up?tags=["kv_cache"]'
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8000/reset_prefix_cache'

# 4. generate; observe metrics:
#    SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00
#    decode ~55 tok/s (vs ~110 baseline)
```

Measured on our box (3-run medians, 256-token generations, ~1k-token prompt):
baseline 111.9 tok/s → post-wake 51.8 tok/s (46% of baseline). A cold
restart of the same config restores full speed, so it is not a config issue.

## Root cause (source-level)

Level 2 sleep discards all weight memory — main model **and drafter** — and
saves only *buffers* to CPU (`gpu_worker.sleep`: `_sleep_saved_buffers` and
`_sleep_saved_draft_buffers` from `named_buffers()`). On wake,
`gpu_worker.wake_up` restores those buffers and re-reserves memory, but the
subsequent `reload_weights` call
(`v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py::reload_weights`) builds its load set from
the **main model's** `named_parameters()`:

```python
model = self.get_model()
weights_to_load = {... for name, _ in model.named_parameters()}
...
loaded_weights = model.load_weights(weights_iterator)
```

`get_draft_model()` (→ `drafter.model`) is a separate module, so the MTP
drafter's parameters are never written after the L2 discard. The drafter
runs on reserved-but-uninitialized memory → acceptance 0 → the verifier
rejects everything → correct outputs at no-spec speed.

The buffer save/restore path already treats main and draft models
symmetrically (`wake_up` lines restoring `_sleep_saved_draft_buffers`); the
parameter reload path simply lacks the symmetric handling.

## Impact

- Silent ~2x decode slowdown after every L2 wake with MTP/EAGLE-style
  speculative decoding (any backend whose drafter is a separate module).
- Model-switch setups (the documented sleep-mode use case) hit this on the
  first swap and never recover without a restart.

## Related

- #29341 (L2 wake produces gibberish main-model outputs — same
  "L2 restore incomplete" family, different layer)
- #16564 (L2 wake weight load failures)
- #28606 (reload_weights issues with quantized formats)
- #46725 (open PR: Runtime Draft Weight Update for Speculative Decoding —
  adjacent machinery)
- #15254 / #30359 (RFCs on wake-up weight-update design)

## Proposed direction

Extend the L2 wake reload path so drafter parameters are reloaded from the
same checkpoint stream (or via the drafter's own load path) before KV-cache
wake. Happy to submit a PR — pointers on preferred shape (extend
`reload_weights` vs. a drafter-specific hook) welcome.

---

*Bug found and reported by an AI agent (Hermes/Aether, operated by Greg
Weyer) during serving-infrastructure debugging; reproduction and source
analysis verified against the installed build.*

items.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- GPU: 2x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (sm120, 96 GB), driver 595.71.05, ECC clean
- Container: `vllm/vllm-openai` v0.26.0 (`sha256:ffb2d59b1c059a5bd8d781320c9f5189de8293693b7d95da54befddaa54abf52`) and v0.27.1 (`sha256:0a51ea5b4ae2dc5d81890e5173f54203d2a3ae0cfffe51b8fd2afd4391bfd967`), podman, `--ipc host`
- CUDA 13.0.2, torch 2.11.0+cu130, flashinfer 0.6.14
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B quantized by ModelOpt 0.47.0.dev0 to `MIXED_PRECISION`. 193 layers NVFP4 (all 64 `mlp.{gate,up,down}_proj` plus `lm_head`), 208 layers FP8 (`linear_attn.*`, `self_attn.*`), `kv_cache_quant_algo: FP8`. Architecture `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` (hybrid GDN linear attention with full attention every 4th layer), hidden 5120, ffn 17408, vocab 248320, 64 layers.
- vLLM resolves this to `quantization=modelopt_mixed` and selects `FlashInferCutlassNvFp4LinearKernel` for the NVFP4 GEMMs, `FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel` for FP8, and the `FLASHINFER` attention backend.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Serving a ModelOpt-NVFP4 checkpoint on SM120 dies under sustained batch load, reliably, on two vLLM releases. The same base model quantized to FP8 and served from the same image with the same attention backend is stable. The failure is specific to the NVFP4 build. I have not isolated the mechanism, and two backends I suspected are now ruled out by measurement (see the update comment below).

**One thing that is measured but is not the cause.** `flashinfer.mm_fp4` hands the CUTLASS FP4 GEMM a fixed 32 MiB shared workspace, and on SM120 the kernel asks for 34 MiB at every M from 1 to 256 for this model's fused gate/up projection (5120 → 34816). Every decode-sized call therefore takes a fallback branch in `csrc/fp4_gemm_cutlass_sm120.cu` that allocates a private workspace and releases it right after an asynchronous launch, including inside CUDA graph capture. That is filed as https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4549 with a fix in https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4550. Raising the shared workspace so the fallback never fires does **not** stop the crash: the patched build failed after 15.0 minutes against 16.5 for the unpatched one. Recording it here so nobody else spends the window I spent on it.

**Symptoms, for searchability.** Two failure modes, both with CUDA graphs enabled:

| vLLM | spec decode | time to failure | error |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.26.0 | none | 16 min 35 s | illegal memory access |
| v0.27.1 | none | 21 min 32 s | illegal memory access |
| v0.26.0 | MTP, 3 tokens | not recorded | misaligned address |
| v0.26.0 | none | 8 s, on a boot right after a prior fault | illegal memory access in `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCache` |

The exception always surfaces at an asynchronous synchronization point, so the reported frame is never the offending kernel:

```
File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py", line 314, in get_output
    self.async_copy_ready_event.synchronize()
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

The second mode is a wedge. The engine stops making progress without raising anything, `/v1/models` still returns 200 in about a millisecond, `/v1/chat/completions` never returns, and the GPU sits at 100% utilization. `py-spy` shows the engine thread blocked in a kernel launch that never returns, and the driver reports `Xid 8 ... GPU is probably locked` only much later. `dmesg` records MMU faults at wild addresses, `faulted @ 0x4_00000000` and `0xf_00001000`, both `FAULT_PDE`.

**Differential.** The same base model quantized to FP8, same box, same image, same FlashInfer attention backend, CUDA graphs on, prefix caching on, `--max-model-len 262144`, logged 10,282 completions across 35 hours with no illegal-address or misaligned-address error. The NVFP4 build dies after roughly 570 completions. Both GPUs produce the NVFP4 fault and ECC is clean on both. `--enforce-eager` reduces the rate roughly tenfold without eliminating it.

We also swept the NVFP4 GEMM for memory-safety problems and found none: every layer shape in the model, every M from 1 to 8192, all 32 SM120 CUTLASS FP4 tactics, under `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` with `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1`, with both a zeroed and a randomly poisoned workspace. Those runs cannot catch this defect, because disabling the caching allocator turns every free into a synchronizing `cudaFree`.

### Workarounds available today from vLLM

Either of these avoids the fallback path without a FlashInfer patch:

1. `VLLM_DISABLED_KERNELS=FlashInferCutlassNvFp4LinearKernel`, which falls through to vLLM's native `CutlassNvFp4LinearKernel`. On our workload that reached 0.65 completions per second against 0.67 for the FlashInfer kernel, and 50 deterministic classification prompts returned byte-identical answers, so the swap does not change results. Soak results below.
2. `--enforce-eager`, which reduces the failure rate roughly tenfold without removing it, and costs more than the kernel swap.

Swapping to `CutlassNvFp4LinearKernel` does not fix the failure, so quarantining the FlashInfer kernel on SM12x would not be a fix either. Both workarounds above are partial.

### 🐛 Describe the bug `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp",...}'` (equivalently `--spec-method qwen3_5_mtp`) fails to load at `--tensor-parallel-size >= 2` for a Qwen3.5-architecture dense model (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, `model_type: qwen3_5`) with a shape-assertion crash inside the MTP drafter's weight loader. It works fine at TP=1 (modulo a separate, likely-unrelated OOM covered at the bottom, on a 24GB GPU specifically). The crash reproduces with both the Qwen3.5-specific and the generic MTP method name, so the method name isn't the variable — it looks like the drafter (loaded via a code path separate from the main model, in `vllm/v1/spec_decode/llm_base_proposer.py`) ends up with an effective tensor-parallel/world size that's inconsistent with the main model's requested TP degree. **Model:** a Heretic-abliterated, NVFP4-quantized (via NVIDIA Model-Optimizer's `hf_ptq.py`, `--qformat nvfp4`) finetune of `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` (dense, `mtp_num_hidden_layers: 1`). The base model's config declares `mtp_use_dedicated_embeddings: false`. Not a MoE model, no `--quantization moe_wna16`/GPTQ/AWQ involved, so this isn't #39475's `moe_wna16` MTP KeyError, and I confirmed `packed_modules_mapping` in `qwen3_5_mtp.py` is correct (`["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj"]` / `["gate_proj","up_proj"]`), so this isn't #35031's `gate_up_proj` copy-paste bug either — those are the two closest prior issues I could find and neither matches. The checkpoint's own `mtp.*` tensors were preserved unmodified from the original release (spliced back in from the raw upstream checkpoint after an unrelated finetuning step dropped them — `transformers`' `Qwen3_5PreTrainedModel._keys_to_ignore_on_load_unexpected = [r"^mtp.*"]` means any `AutoModel.from_pretrained()` round-trip silently discards `mtp.*` weights, so they have to be reattached from the original checkpoint afterward). I want to flag this clearly in case it's relevant, but I don't believe it's the cause of the crash below — see the "ruled out" list. #### Repro ```bash vllm serve \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' ``` Also reproduces identically with `--spec-method qwen3_5_mtp --spec-tokens 3` in place of the JSON `--speculative-config` form. #### Observed ``` (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] param.weight_loader(param, loaded_weight, shard_id) (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] File ".../vllm/model_executor/layers/linear.py", line 989, in weight_loader_v2 (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] param.load_merged_column_weight( (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] File ".../vllm/model_executor/parameter.py", line 175, in load_merged_column_weight (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] assert param_data.shape == loaded_weight.shape (Worker_TP1 ...) ERROR ... [multiproc_executor.py:912] AssertionError ``` Both `Worker_TP0` and `Worker_TP1` crash identically, on the first fused (`qkv_proj` or `gate_up_proj`) weight loaded for the MTP block's single decoder layer (`mtp.layers.0.*`). #### Diagnosis With `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG`, the MTP block's `mlp.down_proj` (a plain row-parallel weight, loaded through a different, less strict code path than the fused-column weights) loads *successfully* right before the crash, with logged shape `torch.Size([5120, 4352])`. The raw checkpoint's `mtp.layers.0.mlp.down_proj.weight` is `(5120, 17408)`. `17408 / 4352 = 4` — not `17408 / 2 = 8704`, which is what correct TP=2 row-parallel sharding should produce. That means the drafter is loading with an effective world size of 4 for at least this tensor, while the rest of the process (main model included) is correctly running at TP=2. The very next fused-column weight for the same MTP layer hits the strict `assert param_data.shape == loaded_weight.shape` in `load_merged_column_weight`, which — unlike `down_proj`'s loader — doesn't tolerate the inconsistency. I wasn't able to pin down exactly where inside `llm_base_proposer.py`'s model/parallel-config construction for `Qwen3_5MultiTokenPredictor` the world size diverges — didn't have a local vLLM checkout set up to add print statements at `get_tensor_model_parallel_world_size()` in the drafter's construction path specifically. The `down_proj` shape is solid, reproducible evidence of *that* the divergence happens; not *why*. #### Ruled out - **Not the method name / CLI form**: identical crash with `--spec-method qwen3_5_mtp` and with the generic `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp",...}'` form. - **Not an NVFP4-quant-exclusion config issue**: tested directly against `ModelOptNvFp4Config.is_layer_excluded()` in a Python shell with the checkpoint's real `hf_quant_config.json` — `mtp.layers.0.self_attn.q_proj` and all sibling MTP linear-layer names correctly resolve as excluded from NVFP4 quantization. The destination parameters are being allocated as plain unquantized `nn.Parameter`s, same as the main model's, so this isn't a quantization-format/exclude-list matching problem. - **Not an actual architecture incompatibility.** I initially assumed the checkpoint's `q_proj` being unusually wide (12288, which is 48 attention-heads'-worth against a nominal 24-head config) was the root cause. That's wrong: the *main* model's decoder layers have the identical `q_proj=(12288,5120)` shape (likely related to `attn_output_gate: true` in the config) and load/serve correctly at TP=2. `Qwen3_5MultiTokenPredictor.__init__` explicitly constructs its single layer via the exact same `Qwen3_5DecoderLayer` class the main model uses for its full-attention layers, so this shape is not MTP-specific and not the bug. - **Disappears entirely at TP=1** — all weight loading succeeds, including everything that crashes at TP=2. (At TP=1 on a single 24GB GPU I then hit a separate `torch.OutOfMemoryError` while constructing `Qwen3_5MTP`'s `ParallelLMHead`, which persisted even after cutting `--max-model-len` from 262144 down to 32768 with no change in the reported memory figures — suggesting the MTP drafter may be allocating its own dedicated `embed_tokens`/`lm_head` regardless of the checkpoint's `mtp_use_dedicated_embeddings: false`, though I haven't confirmed that with an actual memory snapshot at the crash site, just arithmetic that happens to line up — `vocab_size=124160, hidden_size=5120` gives ~1.27GB per duplicated embed/lm_head tensor. Flagging this separately since it may or may not be related; happy to open it as its own issue if it turns out to be unrelated to the TP crash above.)
